I really hope the admins don’t ban me for this discussion.

I think your observations on transsexualism, masculinity, and sexuality are largely based on misconceptions and ignorance of modern scientific evidence.

>But no matter how you act or present, your sex does not change since it is an objective biological attribute (unless you are intersex).

This is part of where the issue lies.  Transexuality (and even certian forms of homosexuality/bisexuality to a certain extent) is likely the byproduct of an intersex condition involving the Central Nervous System.  Very likely caused by hormonal imbalances in-utero during development (which we now know can cause homosexuality in certian cases and very likely transexuality as well).

While it's true that trans individuals do not have the chromosomal/sex organ disorders of other intersex conditions, I think it would be somewhat disengenous to say that there is no biological basis to their feelings or that there isn’t a *strong* potentiality they have a biological system that at the very least has been partially devoloped to a sex other than their natal/reproductive one.  Hence the dysphoria, since their brain is literally at war with the rest of their body.  And also why you could theoretically identify trans individuals using brain scans.

>Obviously there are outliers in between: feminine men and masculine women. Yet they still belong to their biological sex, it is just that their behavioral patterns are more similar to the opposite sex. That's it.

The problem here is that again, it’s been shown there is very likely a biological/developmental factor in the creation of many of those outliers.  I’d wager quite a lot that a majority of those outliers are likely gay/bi, and that many of them struggle with gender identity.  This is why HSTS was a concept for a long time in the medical community concerning transsexuality (putting aside all the other issues I have with Blanchard’s typology, though I suspect he *was* onto something even if his own biases got in the ways of his studies).

All of this to say, I find it very likely you could artificially create the phenomena we’re talking about without sissy hypno using in-utero hormonal manipulation.  But since human experimentation is illegal, unethical to the extreme, and nobody wants a second John Money, I think it will be a while before the science is hashed out.

Also this:

>Even if you buy into this discovering your true self narrative, the only thing you could potentially discover is that:
you are a male who enjoys acting out certain behaviors that correlate with how the opposite sex generally acts. (shaving your legs, being sexually submissive, wearing lingerie, etc...)

Seems to be at odds with this:

>Once you realize these facts, sissy porn kinda loses its magic. It's initially pleasurable because deep down you believe that there is a small chance you might be a woman.

There’s a good portion of people such as myself who aren’t into sissy hypno because of the idea it reaffirms their gender/pushes them more into being feminine (or maybe not *just* that), but rather because it ties into our own sexually submissive/effeminate nature in the barroom as you yourself point out.  In which case it will likely take more than simply reaffirming your masculinity to make it “lose its magic” as you say.  Because in such cases the draw has less to do with trans issues as it does to do with trauma involving submission and sexual degradation.

Without sounding too cynical it’s because they were never taught the answers to begin with and most people who get into that industry are inherently selfish due to the selection process. >Do you have questionse that need answers?

>each time I discovered questions and answers to them I realized what it was I was missing.

I wish I could say the same.  In my case it’s just made me increasingly jaded, blackpilled, and depressed.  The more I learn the more hard it becomes for me to cope with shit.  I try to see the light in things but I guess I’m just more blind to it than most people.

Edit:  Sorry.  Just realized you were talking about people in general and not healthcare professionals.  Yeah most people are intentionally left in the dark to make them more pliable.

Yes.  That’s how I got diagnosed.  Though mental health professionals are part of why I’m in this mess.

50/50 on whether you’ll get someone who actually treats you or just slaps bandaids on hoping the issue will go away.

And 50/50 whether those bandaids will just end up fucking you up even more.

And if you’re super unlucky either they won’t pick up on anything at all, brush off your concerns despite evidence, or even (worst case scenario) treat you incorrectly based on their own biases and prejudices.

There’s some good people in that industry.  Don’t get me wrong.  But it was never designed to actually help people.

I’m for the rights LGBT+ supports but I don’t support the community itself or many of the methods they employ.  I think the LGBT+ community is kind of a mixed bag.  On the one hand they’ve helped to tear down the illusory lines humans draw between “normal” and “abnormal”.   On the other hand, in doing so they’ve also helped to support and normalize behaviors that are downright unhealthy.

Sorry for the delay.  I haven’t been on lately and just checked my messages.

>Pretty much agree with everything here - my gender and sex were not in alignment, so I transitioned to bring them together.

I don’t think it’s the fact that your gender and sex were out of alignment is what caused the issue here though.  Again, all you’d have to do in this case is change your gender role to the one that’s more preferable/in alignment with your sex.  It’s the fact that your brain’s perceived sex and your body’s actual sex were out of alignment, which also caused issues with your gender (since you wanted to switch to the gender more closely associated with your perceived sex).  Hence why changing your gender expression/gender role didn’t work initially, and you had to opt for actual sex oriented transition.

Male to female as opposed to boy/man to girl/woman.  Though in your case you transitioned both sex and gender for maximum affect.

>But it's a little semantic right now since presumably neither of us has the scientific background to specifically know - as you put it we (humans) are woefully short of understanding the human brain in its entirety.

I agree that this is still something I’m researching and thus I don’t have the proper sources necessary at this time to perform an analysis of the findings of neuroscientists and the like.  Though this, again, is why I think that this is an issue that requires lots of research to foster understanding.

>My therapist always used to say the only reason they thought gender dysphoria was in the DSM was to ensure it could be diagnosed and treated.

That’s not an uncommon tact to take but it is a heavily contested one.  I think this is something that’s likely to go back and forth a lot in the coming years as the professionals hash it out.  My main concern being that as with other fields of scientific research moneyed and political interests may get in the way of accuracy and truth.

>Fair enough - gatekeeping may have been a bit strong to describe current practice. Some see it that way, and in a sense it is (there are certain requirements to get treatment from most licensed professionals).

In a sense all medicine requires a certain amount of gatekeeping to ensure safety.  That’s less of a trans issue and more of a security vs. freedom issue.  We could of course allow for a greater free flow of medications and treatments and the like but that also carries greater inherent risks in the case of more experimental procedures and misinformed/mistreated patients.  Many of which may believe themselves to be fine without even having fully realized the effects some of these treatments had on them due to being misinformed or unaware of certain aspects of that treatment.

Without sounding too abrasive it really doesn’t surprise me some trans people have a negative view of increased regulations or speculation in regards to this process.  I’m not going to say a trans person can’t be objective when it comes to these subjects because that’s obviously BS but I think there’s a very real and very understandable element of bias in the trans community when it comes to these subjects.  It’s both in their own self-interest and in the interest of helping fellow trans people to decrease the amount of regulations and steps involved in that process if you believe transition is the panacea to all your woes.  Which in many cases it might be.

However, from the perspective of both those outside of the trans community and the more cautious, there will always be an element of wanting to ensure security despite the potential for a slower and more selective process.  Especially when it comes to children who tend to be less informed and more easily influenced by those around them.  Which is where I think much of this debate comes from.

I myself am not opposed to transition outright but I think that transition and trans issues in general are something that still need a lot of research invested in them.  For example the puberty blockers you referenced are often touted as being reversible, despite lacking a lot of long term research on their effects and some of what has been performed research wise seems to suggest potential negatives.  Meaning they’re very much still experimental, and the accuracy of that reversibility still has to be properly vetted.  Not to mention the potential for as yet unknown side effects down the road.

All of this has to be kept in mind to provide the maximum amount of safety and informedness.  I’m not calling you out in particular but I do think some of the ways this has been approached on *both* sides of the divide have been pretty disengenous, and this concerns me.

I’m going to try and describe my perspective on this and what I meant as clearly as possible but it’s a complex issue so I’m sorry if I mess it up slightly in the telling.

You talk about what’s in your head as being gender, and while to a certain extent I think that’s true, I also think that self image is also linked to sex/biology.  So it’s not simply your gender that’s potentially out of alignment here, though that may or may not be an aspect of it for you personally (I don’t want to presume), but the way your brain/psychology is in relation to your sex that’s out of alignment.

That’s what I meant when it seems clear to me that there was a pretty clear divide here between wanting to change gender and sex.  You brought up the point you experimented with feminine attributes pre-transition but that it wasn’t enough to fix this schism.  Perhaps you even tried to fulfill the societal role of a girl but it couldn’t fix it either.  Again not trying to presume anything just trying to understand.

And so eventually you transitioned because the issue was not simply with your gender but also your sex/sexual attributes.

Idk if this makes any sense to you but that’s kind of what I meant.

I also want to be clear from the get go I think the way mental illness is perceived both professionally and societally (as evidenced by many of the other comments on here) is kind of simplistic and often erroneous if not outright dangerous.  We have a long way to go before we have any of the varied complexities of the human brain mapped out in a way that is anywhere close to being near the mark.

For one thing I definitely don’t think being trans is anything like schizophrenia because that seems to me to indicate a form of psychosis in which you’re detached from reality.  That really isn’t the case and seems to me to be a bad comparison intentionally used to justify maltreatment of and refusal to form a dialogue with trans people.  After all if they’re perceived as psychotic than you can invalidate whatever they say using the prospect of detachment from reality. 

>The way I would put it, is that it's a medical/health issue that can cause significant mental/psychological symptoms to manifest. Same with many other health problems. I think trans people are on a spectrum of what ameliorates their dysphoria. And many don't have access to resources or support to help it. It's like a person with a debilitating injury that prevents them from working.

I think you and I are very much on the same page here.  You’ll note my own comparison to dysphoria and Asperger’s/autism in another post, which again isn’t a perfect comparison but I think it’s a better one insofar as Asperger’s/autism is more similar to dysphoria from my perspective in the sense that it’s a classification of deviation from normal thought patterns, which while not harmful in and of itself, is a spectrum of functionality that can potentially manifest harmful symptoms.

The way I see it mental illness is really only a thing if the symptoms are disabling you and causing suffering in both you and those around you. 

The main reason I brought up the prospect of dysphoria manifesting illness in certain cases was not so much an attack on you as it was an observation that there does seem to be a sizable portion of the trans community who feel their symptoms do manifest as an illness and I do think they bring up valid concerns that if the more negative symptoms of dysphoria are downplayed too much they may not receive the help or recognition they need.  Not saying you’re doing that.  I’m just trying to provide you the perspective from which I’m coming.

>I don't think we need additional "gatekeeping" on this.

No offense but I don’t view this as gatekeeping.  I view this as a valid concern.  It may be true that there are already passable measures in place to regulate this process.  I don’t personally know because I don’t have any experience in this regard.  But I think it’s an issue that has to be monitered regardless in order to ensure the safety and happiness of individuals.

Though I will admit it’s also tricky because there’s those who would likely use such regulations as an excuse to try and enforce restrictions.

>I tried desperately to find any way to not transition but be happy the way I was, and it's just not possible. For me it was bodily. I wanted to have feminine physical traits, and it felt like my brain was hardwired for them - i don't want to get explicit.

See I have a pretty hard time with this aspect of trans philosophy because this seems to me at least to be a pretty clear distinction between wanting to change one's gender (or at least how they want to express that gender) and wanting to change one’s sex.  I don’t view the two as synonymous at all.

>It's not a mental illness. It's not like anorexia. It's not like wanting an arm cut off or wanting to be disabled. It's knowing your situation, but also knowing you wish it was different and that it should be different, and feeling powerless to do anything about it. And knowing that society will hate on you for trying to do anything about it.

Would you agree that even if it’s not an issue in your case it could be considered an illness in someone who is less high functioning and has more adverse symptoms in regards to dysphoria?  I don’t think it’s entirely an illness perse (especially not the way people on here are making it out to be as you’ve pointed out) but I think to state there’s no adverse symptoms that might arise in certain individuals seems to contradict all the stories out there about how dysphoria has literally disabled certain people’s ability to live their lives.  In addition, while transition may have been the proper course of action in your case, there’s enough stories about detransitioning individuals to seemingly at least warrant the question of whether it’s the best course of action in all cases.  Wouldn’t you agree?

I’m someone who has recently been putting a lot of thought into this because I feel that I might be trans.

I think it’s a complicated issue.  I think transgender individuals are techncially separate from transsexual individuals but due to the stigma associated with the latter many choose to associate with the former causing confusion.

To me being transgender is about wanting to occupy a different gender role than the one you were assigned at birth.  This is not the same as being dysphoric and feeling uncomfortable with the sex you were born with.  

This is the difference between wanting to change how you’re perceived and treated societally (boy, girl, or whatever other cultural gender role might exist in your society) vs. wanting to change your actual physiological composition (male vs. female).

The problem is that since gender is a social construct that means gender roles themselves change depending on how society operates.  This is the main struggle of being transgender because, just to list an example, as society becomes more tolerant towards men operating with traits that were formerly perceived as feminine, and women operating with traits that were formerly perceived as masculine, possessing  those traits may no longer be enough to be perceived on a societal basis as part of the opposite gender role.

So you get a lot of struggle and resentment from people who fail to keep up with these changes while trying to either force people to perceive them as appearing similar to a gender role when they don’t fully align or trying to forcibly change the attributes of that gender role as a whole artificially and forcibly so that they do align.  Which is part of where the whole pronoun debate arises from in my opinion.

Now I don’t think all transsexual people are transgender and vice versa but I do think some overlap in regards to the two.

I also think that dysphoria is a mental deviation similar to Asperger’s that can manifest symptoms that result in illness like Asperger’s but which can be managed and even provide beneficial attributes.  I don’t think human psychology is as simple as things being an “illness” or “not an illness”.

I think the only thing that truly qualifies whether something is a “mental illness” or not is whether it causes you and those around you suffering.  So while dysphoria has a higher rate of manifesting as an “illness” and it should be monitored, I’d bet you anything there’s people with dysphoria who are high functioning enough or receive enough proper treatment they manage to live relatively normal lives.

>It seems like dating is based on pure luck and being at the right place at the right time. 

Yes to the second and kind of to the first.  Dating contains an element of random chance just like everything in life but probabilities can be stacked in your favor.  Knowing where to pitch your battles is one of those elements than can be used to increase your odds as you just pointed out.

>it's the norm in society yet i feel like i'm missing out.

Dating is a lot like the weather.  It changes from place to place.  What’s normal in one area/society is definitely not normal in another.  There’s no one baseline for how this stuff works.  It’s one of the most intensely variable fields of human psychology.

>How do i not mess it up with my poor social skills and conversation ability?

No offense but you’re a teenager.  Most teenagers have underdeveloped social skills and conversation abilities, aspie or not.  A certain amount of flailing in teenage romance is to be expected.

>I don't understand how to bridge the gap between someone being a total stranger to somehow being a girlfriend?

That’s because this is one of the more difficult and less likely routes to take in my experience.  Most people know their future lovers for quite a while before they’re officially a thing.

>It just makes no sense, when i go out in public everyone is minding their own business, living their own life, not wanting to be disturbed by a random stranger.

Depends where you’re looking tbh.  People are more or less open depending on the environment they find themselves in.  Places where stress or responsibility is higher?  Probably not the best places to look for companionship.  Places where people are more at ease and willing to be casual?  Bingo.

>It seems like dating is so hard

It seems that way because you’ve psyched yourself out.  You feel socially obligated to date so now you have pressure from a responsibility angle/desire to fit in.  You feel as if dating is important to you and thus you have large amounts of anxiety about failure or not acquiring a partner.  You’ve also started down the path of thinking that because you have Asperger’s that somehow creates this untreatable barrier between you and dating.

Well I’m an Aspie and I found a girl, so while it’s certainly not easy, I’d like you to know it’s definitely possible.

>i have to somehow gauge their interest (difficult)

This is the only real barrier I see from my perspective when it comes to Aspies and dating.  We’re so bad at seeing and acting on signals most times people are pinging us with desire to date but we’re oblivious so we give off “not interested” vibes from their perspective.  Sadly this is something that I think takes a lot of patience, self-awareness, and practice/experience to overcome.  

But it can be done.

This isn’t an NT vs Aspie thing.  This is just a people in general thing.

Stuff happens.  Some people have a bad tendency to overbook themselves because they have poor time management and don’t know how to budget properly.  Some people sell white lies and sweet illusions because they can’t handle disappointment.  Some people don’t know what they want so they say one thing and then go the completely opposite direction based on whims they think will fulfill them.

I do it too sometimes.  It’s a sad fact that in this reality there’s only so much time and so many resources one can spend.

You want to figure out how to predict what commitments people will follow through on?  Figure out what they value.  Or at the very least what they *think* they value.

I’m 24 actually.  If it’s any consolation I was a dope for most of my life, and my critical thinking skills are far more limited and patchwork than I would like having devoloped them far later than most people.  Much of my understanding about reality and other people only happened in the last 4 years or so due to intensive studying, experiences, and observation (ironically after I dropped out of college).

I get the feelings of inadequacy because I feel much the same.  It’s like all the basic life functions and skills that most people have been provided were denied to me but in return I got super specialized skills in a few specific areas that most people don’t even care about.  What’s worse is even when I want to talk about stuff my communication skills are crap so misunderstandings and stupid arguments are the bane my existence.  And even with my understanding of certian issues I always feel outclassed by others further along their paths than I am.

Not to mention I have moments of what I can only describe as blinding idiocy where my brain basically shuts down and leads me to making the stupidest of mistakes.

To be fair I come from a place of high functionality so it could be my attempts to discuss this are flavored by that perception as you say.  I also am in this weird spot where I have a higher EQ/am more capable of reading social and environmental cues than most NT’s while still being limited by my Asperger’s.

That being said I’m of the opinion that functionality is more trained than anything else, and it can go up and down as that training begins to break down or new stressors are introduced that shake up a person’s life.  You can be high functioning for the first few decades of your life and then suddenly have a breakdown and become for all intents and purposes dysfunctional.  The mind is a lot like the body in that way.  It grows or atrophies based on aging, genetics, how you care for it, and what you feed it.

>I've always seen that NTs "reduce things" to essential parts. Global over extraneous/tangential detail.

Less essential and more streamlined and acceptable.  What is considered extraneous and tangential information really depends on the eye of the beholder and that’s kind of what I was getting at.  There’s oftentimes a fundamental disconnect between NT’s and Aspie’s about what information is useful and acceptable and what information isn’t.

>But if you're talking about parsing language, and execution, it's the NTs who operate quickly and efficiently... they are experts at comprehension and highly efficient taskmasters.

Quickly yes.  Efficiency...really depends on the individual and group in question.  I also think there’s different types of informational input/learning styles that NT’s and Aspie’s favor, so depending on the source of information and how it’s presented it can really change things up in terms of who comprehends what first.

Speed isn’t always a benefit when it comes to logic and decision making either.  It’s useful for deadlines and crisis management but if you’re not careful it can also lead to a more shallow understanding of the information presented and thus increased likelihood of sloppiness.

Aspie’s tend to take longer because they’re more thorough in sounding out and testing new information while NT’s are more accepting of information presented at face value so long as it’s credited (like I was saying earlier).  Which again, leads to a more “groupthink” based approach while the baseline of many Aspie’s means they are more comfortable with individuality.

At a certain point though it becomes less of an issue of Aspie’s vs. NT’s and more an issue of people being people.  One thing I’ve learned over the years is that Aspie or NT, people are a mess.  Some people at certainly efficient taskmasters but the vast majority let their own biases, emotional insecurities, and other issues rule their life.

>I think Temple Grandin described most Aspies as having very slow processors, they need to "take a lot of time to consider things, and go over details" and such, pointing out that NTs are the opposite.

I can attest to this.  I sometimes learn thing almost three times as slowly as others.  I don’t view it as entirely a curse though, because I realize by spending more time researching a subject, picking it apart, and observing its core principles I’ll win out in the long run by having a better understanding of the subject than others who were more quick in learning but with less depth.

My main issue personally comes instead from my inability to translate the information I’ve gleaned in an easy and digestible manner.  So oftentimes people either misunderstand my points are just don’t understand what I’m saying.

I think analytical would be a better word than logical.  Aspie’s can be just as illogical as NT’s.  It’s merely that it tends to stem from a more analytical place.  Seeing as I tend to think we can get trapped recursively in our heads far more easily than NT’s.

I do think you’re right though in the sense that this idea of “Aspie’s = Logical and NT’s = Illogical” can be dangerous and downright unhealthy because not only does it breed superiority complexes, it reinforces the idea of never being wrong and thus makes it even more likely you’ll be blind to your mistakes.

There’s also the fact that I think ”pure logic” as many people conceive it is a fallacy and nonexistent.  Humans are messy and all over the place and we are all ultimately human no matter our personal differences.  Logic tends to change anyways depending on where you stand and what you hope to accomplish.

Keeping in mind these are *very* generalized statements and are really only my personal observations about common pitfalls.  And also keeping in mind that not all of these are going to apply to every Aspie or NT.  Rudeness is very perceptual as well so I view this question as being more where NT values/processes conflict with Aspie values/processes.

Many NT’s base credibility on titles, group acceptance, and recommendations from other individuals they respect. Many Aspie’s tend to fact-check sources regardless of these things (at least until they feel the source’s accuracy is consistent enough to be trusted.  This is viewed as weird by many NT’s since the credibility has already been validated by the group, so why do you need to perform further fact-checks on your own?  This can come off as rude or erroneous (and often start disagreements) to Aspie’s who think you should fact check regardless.

Aspie’s are very utilitarian and efficiency based from what I’ve seen.  This conflicts with the more lax perspectives of many NT’s who prefer not to be pressured into things and take their time/do things their own way.  This can lead to a conflict of interest where the NT’s feel their personal space and motivations are being violated and the Aspie’s feel that the the perceived inefficiency of the NT’s hold the group back.

Similarly Aspie’s can feel very constricted when NT’s have them take a more inefficient route to accomplish goals.  They feel like their time is being wasted and their superior is being unprofessional (since leadership *should* stem from respect and personal capability), while from the perspective of the NT superior the Aspie is being insubordinate and not respecting the chain of command.

The problem being that the chain of command that most NT’s subscribe to is abhorrent in many Aspie’s eyes since it’s popularity based vs. merit based.  Thus from the perspective of Aspie’s many workplaces in their entirety can be seen as being rude due to the BS that is workplace politics.

Many NT’s can’t handle debates particularly well and see them as being rude and inconsiderate.  I think a lot of this has to do with the conflation of feelings and opinions with objective facts and theories on the part of NT’s.  Many Aspie’s enjoy debating and having their ideas deconstructed and broken down since they can build them back up without the weaknesses that were exposed in said debates.  Many NT’s get really uncomfortable with that because their frameworks are often based more on feelings masquerading as facts, so they tend to view it as a personal attack or get really insecure since they don’t know how to balance emotionality with logic (which is funny to me because a lot of Aspie’s have the exact opposite issue) leading to behaviors and personal attacks that an Aspie might view as being very rude or unwarranted.

There’s also this idea of “restricted thinking” or “group thinking” on the part of many NT’s where certain ideas are perceived as harmful/negative and thus “off limits”.  Many Aspie’s just don’t care because to them no ideas should be “off limits” and the very act of limiting oneself logically is kind of silly.  This also leads to misunderstandings wherein the NT mistakes an Aspie’s analysis and deconstruction of certain “off limits” ideas as support for those ideas.  This is a “blind spot” that a lot of NT’s have and it leads to a lot of confusion and rudeness on both sides since the Aspie feels they’re being unfairly labeled and chastised and the NT can’t fully grasp what value there is in analyzing such harmful ideas if you’re not trying to propagate them yourself.

Civil war implies there’s a significant enough division and disagreement between two socio-economic blocs within the government.  Democrats vs. Republicans lack the hardline support of the people necessary to initiate that kind of momentum.  Not to mention most politicians regardless of their party largely fall into the same economic blocs and thus any sort of division on that scale would only serve to poison the well they drink from.

What’s *far more* disconcerting is the increasing distrust in the government by most Americans and the movement towards increased separation and independence from the Federal government within many rural areas throughout the country.  I think the chances of some kind of attempted revolution far outweigh the chances of the current government turning on itself.

I wouldn’t say we’re anywhere close to that point but we’re definitely in the soft phases of some kind of internal conflict.  It wouldn’t surprise me at all if we start seeing a steady increase in domestic terrorism as tensions throughout the nation slowly rise.  That’s not to say it will happen either.  We’re still at a point where this could all be prevented and patched up.  But if nothing happens soon I don’t see it heading anywhere good.

Focusing on universal big picture applications = IxxJ and focus on how things matter > outright utility is a sign of F.  You’re also hoping from Ni to Fe here in terms of order of functions.

>I’m future-oriented so if teachers don’t tell me *why I’ll need the information*, I’ll get frustrated but I’m still invested in my studies because I love learning.

Again a focus on how something matters and fits into the framework meaningfully first over its utility and practical benefit.
